questions.q: What does the Calmar ratio measure?
options: Annualized return divided by the standard deviation of daily returns
Annualized return divided by the absolute value of maximum drawdown
The number of winning trades divided by the number of losing trades
Tracking error relative to a benchmark
questions.explain: Calmar = annualized_return / abs(max_drawdown). It measures return earned relative to the single worst peak-to-trough decline, which is why allocators focused on worst-case loss often favor it.

questions.q: What makes the Omega ratio different from the Sharpe and Sortino ratios?
options: Omega can only be computed on monthly data, never daily data
Omega uses the full return distribution split at a threshold, rather than reducing the series to a mean and a standard deviation
Omega ignores all gains and only measures losses
Omega is mathematically identical to Sharpe, just renamed
questions.explain: Sharpe and Sortino summarize a return series using mean and (total or downside) standard deviation. Omega instead sums weighted gains above a threshold against weighted losses below it, using the whole distribution shape rather than just two summary statistics.

questions.q: What does the Information ratio's denominator, "tracking error," actually measure?
options: The strategy's own total return volatility, same as the Sharpe ratio's denominator
The volatility of the difference between the strategy's returns and a benchmark's returns
The number of days the strategy and benchmark moved in the same direction
The maximum drawdown of the benchmark alone
questions.explain: Tracking error is the standard deviation of active return (strategy return minus benchmark return), not the strategy's own volatility in isolation. This is what distinguishes the Information ratio from the Sharpe ratio.

questions.q: A strategy has a perfectly respectable Sharpe ratio but a very low Information ratio versus its benchmark. What does this combination suggest?
options: The Sharpe ratio must have been calculated incorrectly
The strategy has good risk-adjusted absolute returns but is adding little to no consistent value relative to simply holding the benchmark
This combination is mathematically impossible
The strategy's maximum drawdown must be zero
questions.explain: A strategy can show a fine absolute risk-adjusted return (Sharpe) while barely beating, or even just tracking, a benchmark — the Information ratio is specifically designed to reveal this by measuring active, benchmark-relative performance.

questions.q: What is the lesson's recommended discipline for reading a tear sheet with multiple risk-adjusted ratios?
options: Always use whichever ratio produces the highest number, since higher is always better
Ignore all ratios except Sharpe, since it is the only one that matters

Decide in advance which question you're trying to answer (total risk, downside risk, worst-case drawdown, distribution shape, or benchmark-relative performance) before looking at which ratio looks most favorable
Average all the ratios together into one combined score
questions.explain: The lesson warns against picking whichever ratio happens to look best after the fact. Each ratio answers a specific, different question, so the right one to focus on should be chosen based on what you actually want to know, decided before looking at the results.
